claim: Exposure to environmental stress is clinically established to influence male reproductive health.
source: Exposure to environmental stress is clinically established to influence male reproductive health, but the impact of normal cellular metabolism on sperm quality is less well-defined.
evidence: This is a general statement about established clinical knowledge in the field.

claim: Impaired mitochondrial proline catabolism reduces energy-storing flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) levels.
source: Here we show that impaired mitochondrial proline catabolism, reduces energy-storing flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) levels, alters mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion, and leads to age-related loss of sperm quality (size and activity), which diminishes competitive fitness of the animal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of FAD levels in alh-6 mutants shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Impaired mitochondrial proline catabolism alters mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion.
source: Here we show that impaired mitochondrial proline catabolism, reduces energy-storing flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) levels, alters mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion, and leads to age-related loss of sperm quality (size and activity), which diminishes competitive fitness of the animal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased mitochondrial fusion in alh-6 mutant spermatids (Figure 5C-E).

claim: Impaired mitochondrial proline catabolism leads to age-related loss of sperm quality (size and activity).
source: Here we show that impaired mitochondrial proline catabolism, reduces energy-storing flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) levels, alters mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion, and leads to age-related loss of sperm quality (size and activity), which diminishes competitive fitness of the animal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced sperm size (Figure 2B, E) and impaired activation (Figure 2C, F) in alh-6 mutants.

claim: Loss of sperm quality diminishes competitive fitness of the animal.
source: Here we show that impaired mitochondrial proline catabolism, reduces energy-storing flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) levels, alters mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion, and leads to age-related loss of sperm quality (size and activity), which diminishes competitive fitness of the animal.
evidence: This claim is supported by sperm competition assays showing alh-6 mutant males have reduced competitive advantage (Figure 1G).

claim: Loss of the 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate dehydrogenase enzyme alh-6 that catalyzes the second step in mitochondrial proline catabolism leads to premature male reproductive senescence.
source: Loss of the 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate dehydrogenase enzyme alh-6 that catalyzes the second step in mitochondrial proline catabolism leads to premature male reproductive senescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing reduced fertility and sperm defects in alh-6 mutants.

claim: Reducing the expression of the proline catabolism enzyme alh-6 in the germline is sufficient to recapitulate the sperm-related phenotypes observed in alh-6 loss-of-function mutants.
source: Reducing the expression of the proline catabolism enzyme alh-6 or FAD biosynthesis pathway genes in the germline is sufficient to recapitulate the sperm-related phenotypes observed in alh-6 loss-of-function mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by germline-specific RNAi experiments showing impaired sperm activation and increased mitochondrial fusion (Figure 6B-C).

claim: Reducing the expression of FAD biosynthesis pathway genes in the germline is sufficient to recapitulate the sperm-related phenotypes observed in alh-6 loss-of-function mutants.
source: Reducing the expression of the proline catabolism enzyme alh-6 or FAD biosynthesis pathway genes in the germline is sufficient to recapitulate the sperm-related phenotypes observed in alh-6 loss-of-function mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by germline-specific RNAi of R10H10.6 and flad-1 showing reduced sperm activation and increased mitochondrial fusion (Figure 6G-L).

claim: Sperm-specific defects in alh-6 mutants are suppressed by feeding diets that restore FAD levels.
source: These sperm-specific defects are suppressed by feeding diets that restore FAD levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by riboflavin supplementation experiments showing restoration of sperm size and activation (Figure 4F-G).

claim: Decline in oocyte quality is well-documented with age and can result in fertility issues when older couples try to conceive.
source: Decline in oocyte quality is well-documented with age and can result in fertility issues when older couples try to conceive (Baird et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Pregnancies at an older age pose risks for higher incidences of birth defects and miscarriages.
source: Furthermore, pregnancies at an older age pose risks for higher incidences of birth defects and miscarriages.
evidence: This is a statement based on established medical knowledge.

claim: In humans, female reproduction ceases at an average age of 41–60, with the onset of menopause.
source: In humans, female reproduction ceases at an average age of 41–60, with the onset of menopause (Treloar, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Caenorhabditis elegans 'wild type' is hermaphroditic and self-fertilizing.
source: The Caenorhabditis elegans 'wild type' is hermaphroditic and self-fertilizing; however, they are capable of making and maintaining Mendelian ratios of male (sperm-only) animals in their populations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans biology.

claim: C. elegans are capable of making and maintaining Mendelian ratios of male (sperm-only) animals in their populations.
source: The Caenorhabditis elegans 'wild type' is hermaphroditic and self-fertilizing; however, they are capable of making and maintaining Mendelian ratios of male (sperm-only) animals in their populations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans biology.

claim: C. elegans experience a decline in fecundity with age by halting oocyte production at roughly one-third of their lifespan.
source: Like humans, C. elegans experience a decline in fecundity with age by halting oocyte production at roughly one-third of their lifespan (Kadandale and Singson, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Regulators of reproductive aging, such as insulin/IGF-1 and sma-2/TGF-β signaling, are conserved regulators of reproductive aging from worms to humans.
source: In addition, regulators of reproductive aging, such as insulin/IGF-1 and sma-2/TGF-β signaling, are conserved regulators of reproductive aging from worms to humans (Luo et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Male factors contribute to a large portion of fertility complications with increasing evidence of an inverse relationship between paternal age and sperm health.
source: While the majority of studies in reproductive senescence have focused on maternal effects, male factors contribute to a large portion of fertility complications with increasing evidence of an inverse relationship between paternal age and sperm health (Lemaître and Gaillard, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Studies in mammals have shown an age-related decline in sperm quality with increased incidences of DNA damage, reduced motility, abnormal morphology, and decreased semen volume.
source: In fact, studies in mammals have shown an age-related decline in sperm quality with increased incidences of DNA damage, reduced motility, abnormal morphology, and decreased semen volume (Cocuzza et al., 2008; Kidd et al., 2001; Ozkosem et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) is an important cofactor that participates in enzymatic redox reactions that are used in cellular metabolism and homeostasis.
source: Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) is an important cofactor that participates in enzymatic redox reactions that are used in cellular metabolism and homeostasis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: FAD is synthesized from riboflavin by the concerted actions of FAD synthetase and riboflavin kinase.
source: FAD is synthesized from riboflavin by the concerted actions of FAD synthetase and riboflavin kinase.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about FAD biosynthesis.

claim: C. elegans cannot synthesize riboflavin, and therefore requires dietary intake.
source: Like humans, C. elegans cannot synthesize riboflavin, and therefore requires dietary intake (Braeckman, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Humans cannot synthesize riboflavin.
source: Like humans, C. elegans cannot synthesize riboflavin, and therefore requires dietary intake (Braeckman, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about human metabolism.

claim: Disruption of flavin homeostasis in humans and animal models has been associated with several diseases, including: cardiovascular diseases, cancer, anemia, abnormal fetal development, and neuromuscular and neurological disorders.
source: Disruption of flavin homeostasis in humans and animal models has been associated with several diseases, including: cardiovascular diseases, cancer, anemia, abnormal fetal development, and neuromuscular and neurological disorders (Barile et al., 2013); however, the link between FAD homeostasis and fertility is undefined.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The link between FAD homeostasis and fertility is undefined.
source: Disruption of flavin homeostasis in humans and animal models has been associated with several diseases, including: cardiovascular diseases, cancer, anemia, abnormal fetal development, and neuromuscular and neurological disorders (Barile et al., 2013); however, the link between FAD homeostasis and fertility is undefined.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in current knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: Age-specific female reproductive success strongly depends on male–female interactions.
source: We demonstrate that, although reproductive senescence is generally studied only from the female viewpoint, age-speciﬁc female reproductive success strongly depends on male–female interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mating experiments showing that wild-type males can rescue fertility of alh-6 hermaphrodites (Figure 1F).

claim: A reduction in male fertilization efficiency with increasing age has detrimental consequences for female fitness.
source: Thus, a reduction in male fertilization efﬁciency with increasing age has detrimental consequences for female ﬁtness.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced fertility when hermaphrodites mate with alh-6 mutant males.

claim: Mutation in nuo-1, a complex I component of the mitochondria respiratory chain, results in reduced brood size caused by impaired germline development.
source: Mutation in nuo-1, a complex I component of the mitochondria respiratory chain, results in reduced brood size caused by impaired germline development (Grad and Lemire, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: clk-1 mutation affects the timing of egg laying, resulting in reduced brood size.
source: Similarly, clk-1 mutation affects the timing of egg laying, resulting in reduced brood size (Jonassen et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: alh-6 is the C. elegans ortholog of human ALDH4A1.
source: alh-6, the C. elegans ortholog of human ALDH4A1, is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial enzyme that functions in the second step of the proline metabolism pathway, converting 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C) to glutamate (Adams and Frank, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature establishing the orthology.

claim: alh-6 is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial enzyme that functions in the second step of the proline metabolism pathway, converting 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C) to glutamate.
source: alh-6, the C. elegans ortholog of human ALDH4A1, is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial enzyme that functions in the second step of the proline metabolism pathway, converting 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C) to glutamate (Adams and Frank, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and established biochemical knowledge.

claim: alh-6(lax105) loss-of-function mutants display altered mitochondrial structure in the muscle accompanied by increased level of ROS in adult animals.
source: We previously revealed that alh-6(lax105) loss-of-function mutants display altered mitochondrial structure in the muscle accompanied by increased level of ROS in adult animals (Pang and Curran, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Mutation in alh-6 results in the activation of SKN-1/NRF2.
source: Furthermore, mutation in alh-6 results in the activation of SKN-1/NRF2 (Pang et al., 2014), an established regulator of oxidative stress response, likely through the accumulation of toxic P5C disrupting mitochondrial homeostasis (Pang and Curran, 2014; Pang et al., 2014; Deuschle et al., 2004; Miller et al., 2009; Nomura and Takagi, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SKN-1/NRF2 is an established regulator of oxidative stress response.
source: Furthermore, mutation in alh-6 results in the activation of SKN-1/NRF2 (Pang et al., 2014), an established regulator of oxidative stress response, likely through the accumulation of toxic P5C disrupting mitochondrial homeostasis (Pang and Curran, 2014; Pang et al., 2014; Deuschle et al., 2004; Miller et al., 2009; Nomura and Takagi, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SKN-1/NRF2 function.

claim: Accumulation of toxic P5C disrupts mitochondrial homeostasis.
source: Furthermore, mutation in alh-6 results in the activation of SKN-1/NRF2 (Pang et al., 2014), an established regulator of oxidative stress response, likely through the accumulation of toxic P5C disrupting mitochondrial homeostasis (Pang and Curran, 2014; Pang et al., 2014; Deuschle et al., 2004; Miller et al., 2009; Nomura and Takagi, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SKN-1 responds to accumulation of damaged mitochondria by inducing their biogenesis and degradation through autophagy.
source: Interestingly, SKN-1 was recently shown to respond to accumulation of damaged mitochondria by inducing their biogenesis and degradation through autophagy (Palikaras et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Altered mitochondrial structure and activity have been correlated with sperm dysfunction across different species.
source: Altered mitochondrial structure and activity have been correlated with sperm dysfunction across different species (Liau et al., 2007; Amaral et al., 2013; Ramalho-Santos and Amaral, 2013; Nakada et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Proper sperm function requires low levels of ROS.
source: In addition, proper sperm function requires low levels of ROS (de Lamirande and Gagnon, 1993; Kodama et al., 1996; Leclerc et al., 1997), although a specific role for endogenous mitochondrial derived ROS is undefined.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A specific role for endogenous mitochondrial derived ROS in sperm function is undefined.
source: In addition, proper sperm function requires low levels of ROS (de Lamirande and Gagnon, 1993; Kodama et al., 1996; Leclerc et al., 1997), although a specific role for endogenous mitochondrial derived ROS is undefined.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in current knowledge.

claim: ALH-6 localizes to the mitochondria in the germline of both hermaphrodites and males.
source: Using an UV-integrated alh-6::gfp strain under its endogenous promoter, we saw that ALH-6 localizes to the mitochondria in the germline of both hermaphrodites and males (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data showing GFP localization in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: alh-6(lax105) hermaphrodites fed the standard OP50/E. coli B strain diet show a reduction in self-fertility brood size (−12.9%).
source: We then assessed progeny output of alh-6(lax105) hermaphrodites fed the standard OP50/E. coli B strain diet and found a reduction in self-fertility brood size (−12.9%) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The self-fertility of alh-6 animals fed the HT115 diet is markedly reduced (−20.7%).
source: Surprisingly, we found that the self-fertility of alh-6 animals was markedly reduced (−20.7%), when animals were fed the HT115 diet (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: alh-6 mutants have similar timing in their progeny output as compared to wild type animals on both diets.
source: alh-6 mutants have similar timing in their progeny output as compared to wild type animals on both diets (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: alh-6 mutants display normal development and reproductive timing.
source: Since alh-6 mutants display normal development and reproductive timing, the progeny deficit is not a result of an attenuated reproductive span which reveals the differential impact of alh-6 loss in the soma (diet-dependent) (Pang and Curran, 2014) and the germline (diet-independent).
evidence: This claim is supported by the timing data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The progeny deficit in alh-6 mutants is not a result of an attenuated reproductive span.
source: Since alh-6 mutants display normal development and reproductive timing, the progeny deficit is not a result of an attenuated reproductive span which reveals the differential impact of alh-6 loss in the soma (diet-dependent) (Pang and Curran, 2014) and the germline (diet-independent).
evidence: This is inferred from the normal reproductive timing data.

claim: alh-6 loss has differential impact in the soma (diet-dependent) and the germline (diet-independent).
source: Since alh-6 mutants display normal development and reproductive timing, the progeny deficit is not a result of an attenuated reproductive span which reveals the differential impact of alh-6 loss in the soma (diet-dependent) (Pang and Curran, 2014) and the germline (diet-independent).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing somatic phenotypes (diet-dependent) with germline phenotypes (diet-independent) and a citation to prior work.

claim: alh-6 mutant hermaphrodite animals laid twice as many unfertilized oocytes as wild type animals over their reproductive-span.
source: We noted that alh-6 mutant hermaphrodite animals laid twice as many unfertilized oocytes as wild type animals over their reproductive-span (Figure 1D), suggesting an impairment of sperm function (McCarter et al., 1999; Ward and Miwa, 1978; Argon and Ward, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Increased unfertilized oocytes in alh-6 mutants suggests an impairment of sperm function.
source: We noted that alh-6 mutant hermaphrodite animals laid twice as many unfertilized oocytes as wild type animals over their reproductive-span (Figure 1D), suggesting an impairment of sperm function (McCarter et al., 1999; Ward and Miwa, 1978; Argon and Ward, 1980).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: alh-6 mutant hermaphrodites lay very few, if any, dead eggs.
source: It is notable that alh-6 mutant hermaphrodites lay very few, if any, dead eggs (Figure 1D), suggesting that the loss of ALH-6 activity is not lethal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The loss of ALH-6 activity is not lethal.
source: It is notable that alh-6 mutant hermaphrodites lay very few, if any, dead eggs (Figure 1D), suggesting that the loss of ALH-6 activity is not lethal.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that very few dead eggs are laid.

claim: The reduced fertility in alh-6 mutant hermaphrodites is fully rescued by wild type sperm.
source: We found that the reduced fertility in alh-6 mutant hermaphrodites is fully rescued by wild type sperm, which confirmed that oocyte quality is not impaired but rather, alh-6 hermaphrodite sperm appears to be dysfunctional (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Oocyte quality is not impaired in alh-6 mutants.
source: We found that the reduced fertility in alh-6 mutant hermaphrodites is fully rescued by wild type sperm, which confirmed that oocyte quality is not impaired but rather, alh-6 hermaphrodite sperm appears to be dysfunctional (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment showing that wild-type sperm can restore fertility.

claim: alh-6 hermaphrodite sperm appears to be dysfunctional.
source: We found that the reduced fertility in alh-6 mutant hermaphrodites is fully rescued by wild type sperm, which confirmed that oocyte quality is not impaired but rather, alh-6 hermaphrodite sperm appears to be dysfunctional (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment and supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: In C. elegans wild type animals, male sperm are larger and faster than hermaphrodite sperm, which affords a competitive advantage.
source: In C. elegans wild type animals, male sperm are larger and faster than hermaphrodite sperm, which affords a competitive advantage (LaMunyon and Ward, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Wild type hermaphrodites when mated to alh-6 mutant males have significantly more self-sperm-derived progeny as compared to those mated to wild type males.
source: We found that wild type hermaphrodites when mated to alh-6 mutant males have significantly more self-sperm-derived progeny as compared to those mated to wild type males (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: alh-6 male sperm have a competition deficit resulting in increased proportion of progeny derived from hermaphrodite sperm.
source: This finding indicates a competition deficit of alh-6 male sperm resulting in this increased proportion of progeny derived from hermaphrodite sperm, which is uncommon after mating has occurred (Ward and Carrel, 1979).
evidence: This is inferred from the competition assay data and supported by a citation.

claim: C. elegans hermaphrodites produce a set amount of sperm exclusively at the L4 developmental stage, before switching exclusively to oogenesis.
source: C. elegans hermaphrodites produce a set amount of sperm exclusively at the L4 developmental stage, before switching exclusively to oogenesis. As such, hermaphrodites eventually deplete their reservoir of sperm (Hirsh et al., 1976; Ward and Carrel, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hermaphrodites eventually deplete their reservoir of sperm.
source: C. elegans hermaphrodites produce a set amount of sperm exclusively at the L4 developmental stage, before switching exclusively to oogenesis. As such, hermaphrodites eventually deplete their reservoir of sperm (Hirsh et al., 1976; Ward and Carrel, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: alh-6 mutant males are able to produce equal numbers of progeny as wild type males when the need for competition with hermaphrodite sperm is abated.
source: To assess whether alh-6 mutant sperm are generally dysfunctional, we mated older hermaphrodites that had depleted their complement of self-sperm and found that alh-6 mutant males are able to produce equal numbers of progeny as wild type males when the need for competition with hermaphrodite sperm is abated (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A); thus, although alh-6 mutant sperm are impaired for competition, they remain viable for reproduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: alh-6 mutant sperm are impaired for competition but remain viable for reproduction.
source: To assess whether alh-6 mutant sperm are generally dysfunctional, we mated older hermaphrodites that had depleted their complement of self-sperm and found that alh-6 mutant males are able to produce equal numbers of progeny as wild type males when the need for competition with hermaphrodite sperm is abated (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A); thus, although alh-6 mutant sperm are impaired for competition, they remain viable for reproduction.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing equal progeny numbers when competition is removed.

claim: Older sperm-depleted alh-6 mutant hermaphrodites produced similar brood sizes when mated to young wild type or alh-6 mutant males.
source: Similarly, older sperm-depleted alh-6 mutant hermaphrodites produced similar brood sizes when mated to young wild type or alh-6 mutant males, which further supports a model where sperm, but not oocytes, are defective in alh-6 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Sperm, but not oocytes, are defective in alh-6 mutants.
source: Similarly, older sperm-depleted alh-6 mutant hermaphrodites produced similar brood sizes when mated to young wild type or alh-6 mutant males, which further supports a model where sperm, but not oocytes, are defective in alh-6 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from multiple experimental results showing that oocytes are functional but sperm are defective.

claim: The contribution of sperm to fertility in C. elegans is dictated by distinct functional qualities, which include: sperm number, size, and motility.
source: Similar to mammals, the contribution of sperm to fertility in C. elegans is dictated by distinct functional qualities, which include: sperm number, size, and motility (Ward and Miwa, 1978; LaMunyon and Ward, 2002; LaMunyon and Ward, 1998; Singson et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One day after the onset of spermatogenesis, alh-6 adult hermaphrodites have a reduced number of sperm in the spermatheca as compared to wild type.
source: One day after the onset of spermatogenesis (at the L4 larval stage of development), alh-6 adult hermaphrodites have a reduced number of sperm in the spermatheca as compared to wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which is correlated with the reduced self-fertility observed (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Age-matched alh-6 mutant virgin males have similar numbers of spermatids as WT virgin males.
source: In contrast, age-matched alh-6 mutant virgin males have similar numbers of spermatids as WT virgin males, suggesting that they have a similar rate of production (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: alh-6 mutant males have a similar rate of spermatid production as wild-type males.
source: In contrast, age-matched alh-6 mutant virgin males have similar numbers of spermatids as WT virgin males, suggesting that they have a similar rate of production (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that spermatid numbers are similar.

claim: alh-6 mutant spermatids are significantly smaller as compared to wild type in day one adult males.
source: We next examined sperm size in day one adult males and discovered that alh-6 mutant spermatids are significantly smaller as compared to wild type (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: C. elegans spermatids must form a pseudopod to achieve motility, which requires protease activation.
source: To achieve motility, C. elegans spermatids must form a pseudopod which requires protease activation (Ward et al., 1983; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Sperm activation can be recapitulated in vitro by treatment of isolated spermatids with the Streptomyces griseus protease Pronase.
source: Sperm activation can be recapitulated in vitro by treatment of isolated spermatids with the Streptomyces griseus protease Pronase (Shakes and Ward, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: After 30 min of Pronase treatment, 80% of wildtype spermatids are fully activated, while a significantly reduced population of alh-6 mutant spermatids mature over the same time period.
source: After 30 min of Pronase treatment, 80% of wildtype spermatids are fully activated, while a significantly reduced population of alh-6 mutant spermatids mature over the same time period (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The reduction in activation in alh-6 mutant spermatids is correlated with an increase in the number of cells observed at the normally transient intermediate stage of spermiogenesis characterized by the presence of 'spikes'.
source: The reduction in activation, as measured by the presence of a fully extended pseudopod, in alh-6 mutant spermatids is correlated with an increase in the number of cells observed at the normally transient intermediate stage of spermiogenesis characterized by the presence of 'spikes' (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C; Shakes and Ward, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C and a citation.

claim: alh-6 mutant spermatids were stalled at the 'protrusion' intermediate stage of spermiogenesis when treated with Monensin.
source: We observed a similar impairment in activation of alh-6 mutant spermatids when treated with the cationic ionophore Monensin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E), except that alh-6 mutant spermatids were stalled at the 'protrusion' intermediate stage of spermiogenesis (Nelson and Ward, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E and a citation.

claim: Sperm number was reduced in alh-6 mutant males fed HT115 diet compared to age-matched WT males on the same diet.
source: Interestingly, although sperm number was the same between WT and alh-6 mutant males on the OP50 diet, sperm number was reduced in alh-6 mutant males fed HT115 diet compared to age-matched WT males on the same diet (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Spermatids from alh-6 mutant males raised on the HT115 diet were defective in size and activation.
source: We also noted that spermatids from alh-6 mutant males raised on the HT115 diet were similarly defective in size and activation (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E–F.

claim: Although diet can influence sperm number, the reduction of sperm size and activation are likely contributors to the reduced fertility and competitive fitness in alh-6 mutant males, which is independent of diet.
source: Taken together, although diet can influence sperm number, the reduction of sperm size and activation are likely contributors to the reduced fertility and competitive fitness in alh-6 mutant males; which is independent of diet.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sperm size and activation defects occur on both diets.

claim: alh-6 mutants display progeroid phenotypes towards the end of the normal reproductive span.
source: alh-6 mutants have normal development, but display progeroid phenotypes towards the end of the normal reproductive span (Pang and Curran, 2014) indicating a temporal switch in phenotypic outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SKN-1 is activated in alh-6 mutants after day 2 of adulthood.
source: As SKN-1 is activated in alh-6 mutants after day 2 of adulthood (Pang and Curran, 2014), we defined genes that display differentially altered expression in the L4 developmental stage, when spermatogenesis occurs, as compared to day three adults (post SKN-1 activation).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: 1935 genes in L4 stage animals are differentially expressed in alh-6 mutants compared to wild-type.
source: We performed RNA-Seq analyses of worms with loss of alh-6 and identified 1935 genes in L4 stage animals and 456 genes in day three adult animals that are differentially expressed (+/- Log2 (fold change), 0.05 FDR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: 456 genes in day three adult animals are differentially expressed in alh-6 mutants compared to wild-type.
source: We performed RNA-Seq analyses of worms with loss of alh-6 and identified 1935 genes in L4 stage animals and 456 genes in day three adult animals that are differentially expressed (+/- Log2 (fold change), 0.05 FDR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The gene expression changes at L4 and day three adult life periods had distinct transcriptional signatures.
source: Notably, the gene expression changes at these two life periods had distinct transcriptional signatures (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 3A–B.

claim: The Gene Ontology (GO) terms most enriched in L4 stage animals include oxidoreductases and metabolic enzymes.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, the Gene Ontology (GO) terms most enriched include oxidoreductases and metabolic enzymes in L4 stage animals (Figure 3A) and SKN-1-dependent targets such as glutathione metabolism pathway genes in day three adults (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Gene Ontology (GO) terms most enriched in day three adults include SKN-1-dependent targets such as glutathione metabolism pathway genes.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, the Gene Ontology (GO) terms most enriched include oxidoreductases and metabolic enzymes in L4 stage animals (Figure 3A) and SKN-1-dependent targets such as glutathione metabolism pathway genes in day three adults (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Genes in the pseudopodium and germ plasm GO terms class displayed reduced expression in L4 alh-6 mutant animals.
source: Importantly, our transcriptomic analysis recapitulated the temporally-dependent phenotypic outcomes resulting from alh-6 loss; genes in the pseudopodium and germ plasm GO terms class displayed reduced expression in L4 alh-6 mutant animals (Figure 3A), which include many genes in the major sperm protein (MSP) family that comprises 15% of total protein content in C. elegans sperm and impact sperm function (Klass and Hirsh, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Many genes in the major sperm protein (MSP) family comprise 15% of total protein content in C. elegans sperm and impact sperm function.
source: Importantly, our transcriptomic analysis recapitulated the temporally-dependent phenotypic outcomes resulting from alh-6 loss; genes in the pseudopodium and germ plasm GO terms class displayed reduced expression in L4 alh-6 mutant animals (Figure 3A), which include many genes in the major sperm protein (MSP) family that comprises 15% of total protein content in C. elegans sperm and impact sperm function (Klass and Hirsh, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Genes in the muscle-specific GO term class displayed increased expression in day three adults.
source: In contrast, genes in the muscle-specific GO term class displayed increased expression in day three adults (Figure 3B), which is when activation of the SKN-1 reporter is enhanced in the muscle of alh-6 mutants (Pang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Activation of the SKN-1 reporter is enhanced in the muscle of alh-6 mutants at day three adulthood.
source: In contrast, genes in the muscle-specific GO term class displayed increased expression in day three adults (Figure 3B), which is when activation of the SKN-1 reporter is enhanced in the muscle of alh-6 mutants (Pang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The proline catabolism pathway utilizes multiple cofactors to generate glutamate from proline.
source: In fact, the proline catabolism pathway utilizes multiple cofactors to generate glutamate from proline; PRDH-1 uses FAD as a co-factor to convert proline to P5C while ALH-6 utilizes the reduction of NAD+ to convert P5C to glutamate.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the proline catabolism pathway.

claim: PRDH-1 uses FAD as a co-factor to convert proline to P5C.
source: In fact, the proline catabolism pathway utilizes multiple cofactors to generate glutamate from proline; PRDH-1 uses FAD as a co-factor to convert proline to P5C while ALH-6 utilizes the reduction of NAD+ to convert P5C to glutamate.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about PRDH-1 function.

claim: ALH-6 utilizes the reduction of NAD+ to convert P5C to glutamate.
source: In fact, the proline catabolism pathway utilizes multiple cofactors to generate glutamate from proline; PRDH-1 uses FAD as a co-factor to convert proline to P5C while ALH-6 utilizes the reduction of NAD+ to convert P5C to glutamate.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about ALH-6 function.

claim: In the absence of ALH-6, accumulation of P5C drives the expression of pathways to detoxify P5C.
source: Additionally, in the absence of ALH-6, accumulation of P5C, the toxic metabolic intermediate of proline catabolism, drives the expression of pathways to detoxify P5C (oxidoreductases, P5C reductase, etc.) (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FAD levels are significantly reduced in alh-6 mutant animals fed the OP50 diet at the L4 stage.
source: We measured FAD and found a significant reduction in alh-6 mutant animals fed the OP50 diet at the L4 stage (Figure 4B) and a similar reduction in animals fed HT115 bacteria at L4 stage (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: FAD levels are significantly reduced in alh-6 mutant animals fed HT115 bacteria at L4 stage.
source: We measured FAD and found a significant reduction in alh-6 mutant animals fed the OP50 diet at the L4 stage (Figure 4B) and a similar reduction in animals fed HT115 bacteria at L4 stage (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Differences in FAD levels were unremarkable in day three adult animals.
source: Differences in FAD levels were unremarkable in day three adult animals, when spermatogenesis has long since ended (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Riboflavin supplementation to the OP50 diet of alh-6 mutants restored FAD levels to wild-type levels.
source: Similarly, riboflavin supplementation to the OP50 diet of alh-6 mutants restored FAD levels to wild-type levels (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Wild type hermaphrodites mated to alh-6 mutant males fed a riboflavin supplemented diet produced significantly more total progeny than alh-6 males fed the standard OP50 diet.
source: We found that wild type hermaphrodites mated to alh-6 mutant males fed a riboflavin supplemented diet produced significantly more total progeny than alh-6 males fed the standard OP50 diet (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Riboflavin supplementation was sufficient to partially restore male sperm size in alh-6 mutants.
source: Moreover, riboflavin supplementation was sufficient to partially restore male sperm size (Figure 4F) and also rescued the impaired activation (Figure 4G) of male sperm in alh-6 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Riboflavin supplementation rescued the impaired activation of male sperm in alh-6 mutants.
source: Moreover, riboflavin supplementation was sufficient to partially restore male sperm size (Figure 4F) and also rescued the impaired activation (Figure 4G) of male sperm in alh-6 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Riboflavin supplementation increases sperm size in WT males.
source: Riboflavin supplementation increases sperm size in WT males, but do not change sperm activation in WT males (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Riboflavin supplementation does not change sperm activation in WT males.
source: Riboflavin supplementation increases sperm size in WT males, but do not change sperm activation in WT males (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: RNAi knockdown of R10H10.6 in WT males reduces their sperm size compared to L4440 vector control.
source: We used RNA interference (RNAi) against R10H10.6 or flad-1 in wild-type male animals and measured sperm quality. Similar to alh-6 mutant sperm, RNAi reduction of the FAD biosynthetic pathway decreased sperm size (Figure 4H and I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F) and impaired sperm activation (Figure 4J and K, Figures Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: RNAi knockdown of flad-1 in WT males reduces their sperm size compared to L4440 vector control.
source: We used RNA interference (RNAi) against R10H10.6 or flad-1 in wild-type male animals and measured sperm quality. Similar to alh-6 mutant sperm, RNAi reduction of the FAD biosynthetic pathway decreased sperm size (Figure 4H and I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F) and impaired sperm activation (Figure 4J and K, Figures Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: RNAi knockdown of R10H10.6 in WT males impairs sperm activation.
source: We used RNA interference (RNAi) against R10H10.6 or flad-1 in wild-type male animals and measured sperm quality. Similar to alh-6 mutant sperm, RNAi reduction of the FAD biosynthetic pathway decreased sperm size (Figure 4H and I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F) and impaired sperm activation (Figure 4J and K, Figures Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: RNAi knockdown of flad-1 in WT males impairs sperm activation.
source: We used RNA interference (RNAi) against R10H10.6 or flad-1 in wild-type male animals and measured sperm quality. Similar to alh-6 mutant sperm, RNAi reduction of the FAD biosynthetic pathway decreased sperm size (Figure 4H and I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F) and impaired sperm activation (Figure 4J and K, Figures Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: NAD and NADH levels and their ratio are unremarkable between wild-type and alh-6 mutant animals.
source: NAD+ and NADH are also central adenine dinucleotide cofactors that play critical roles in metabolism and have received recent attention as a method to combat the decline seen in biological function with age (Guarente, 2016). As such, we also measured NAD and NADH levels, but found the ratio unremarkable between wild-type and alh-6 mutant animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: Loss of alh-6 leads to a specific decrease in cellular FAD levels.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that loss of alh-6 leads to a specific decrease in cellular FAD levels and that FAD is a critical cofactor that drives proper sperm function.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced FAD levels in alh-6 mutants.

claim: FAD is a critical cofactor that drives proper sperm function.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that loss of alh-6 leads to a specific decrease in cellular FAD levels and that FAD is a critical cofactor that drives proper sperm function.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with riboflavin and the phenocopy of sperm defects with FAD biosynthesis RNAi.

claim: Each wild type spermatid on average contained multiple discernable spherical mitochondria that are mostly not fused.
source: We first examined mitochondrial dynamics in wild type spermatids by staining with the fluorescent mitochondrial-specific dye JC-1, and noted that each spermatid on average contained multiple discernable spherical mitochondria that are mostly not fused (Figure 5A, B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A, B and E.

claim: When cells are exposed to mild stress, the initial response of mitochondria is to fuse in order to dilute damage.
source: Previous studies in yeast and cultured mammalian cells have shown that when cells are exposed to mild stress, the initial response of mitochondria is to fuse in order to dilute damage (Tondera et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2011; Rambold et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: alh-6 mutant spermatids have reduced JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratio, indicating mitochondria depolarization.
source: The mitochondrial specific dye JC-1 accumulates in mitochondria in a membrane potential-dependent manner, and as the concentration increases, its fluorescence switches from green to red emission. The accumulation of sufficient JC-1 molecules required for red emission is abolished by treatment with Carbonyl cyanide m-chlorophenyl hydrazone (CCCP), a chemical inhibitor of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A). Therefore, a higher red-to-green fluorescence ratio in cells is indicative of healthier mitochondria species and as such, we characterized mitochondria with red JC-1 emission in our analyses of connectivity in spermatids. alh-6 mutant spermatids have reduced red:green JC-1 fluorescence that indicates a lower mitochondrial membrane potential and an accumulation of unhealthy mitochondria (Figure 5F; Smiley et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: alh-6 mutant spermatids have mitochondria that were more interconnected as compared to wild type spermatids.
source: Moreover, alh-6 mutant spermatids have mitochondria that were more interconnected (Figure 5C–E) as compared to wild type spermatids and a similar increase in connectivity was observed when mitochondria were visualized with the membrane potential-dependent mitochondrial dye Mitotracker Red CMXRos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C–E.

claim: The increase in fused mitochondria in spermatids was also present in animals fed the HT115 diet.
source: The increase in fused mitochondria in spermatids was also present in animals fed the HT115 diet, which further supports a diet-independent role for alh-6 in the germline (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RNAi targeting R10H10.6 resulted in more connected mitochondria that resembles the increased fusion in alh-6 mutant spermatids.
source: We first reduced FAD biosynthesis with RNAi targeting R10H10.6 or flad-1, which resulted in more connected mitochondria that resembles the increased fusion in alh-6 mutant spermatids that are under metabolic stress (Figure 5G–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: RNAi targeting flad-1 resulted in more connected mitochondria that resembles the increased fusion in alh-6 mutant spermatids.
source: We first reduced FAD biosynthesis with RNAi targeting R10H10.6 or flad-1, which resulted in more connected mitochondria that resembles the increased fusion in alh-6 mutant spermatids that are under metabolic stress (Figure 5G–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Increasing FAD levels by dietary supplementation of riboflavin restored mitochondria in spermatids of alh-6 animals to more wild-type-like distributions.
source: In addition, increasing FAD levels by dietary supplementation of riboflavin, restored mitochondria in spermatids of alh-6 animals to more wild-type-like distributions (Figure 5I), but did not change mitochondrial morphology in WT male spermatids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Riboflavin supplementation did not change mitochondrial morphology in WT male spermatids.
source: In addition, increasing FAD levels by dietary supplementation of riboflavin, restored mitochondria in spermatids of alh-6 animals to more wild-type-like distributions (Figure 5I), but did not change mitochondrial morphology in WT male spermatids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The homeostatic control of FAD level is critical to maintain proper mitochondrial dynamics in sperm.
source: Thus, the reduction of FAD in alh-6 mutants, alters mitochondrial dynamics to a more fused and less punctate state. Therefore, the homeostatic control of FAD level is critical to maintain proper mitochondrial dynamics in sperm.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that FAD levels affect mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: The mitochondrial fusion and fission machinery are important for the elimination of paternal mitochondria post-fertilization.
source: The role of mitochondrial dynamics in the maturation of sperm has not been studied; however recent work has revealed that the mitochondrial fusion and fission machinery are important for the elimination of paternal mitochondria post-fertilization (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: FZO-1 is required for proper fusion of the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source: FZO-1 is required for proper fusion of the mitochondrial outer membrane while EAT-3/OPA1 regulates inner membrane fusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial fusion machinery.

claim: EAT-3/OPA1 regulates inner membrane fusion.
source: FZO-1 is required for proper fusion of the mitochondrial outer membrane while EAT-3/OPA1 regulates inner membrane fusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial fusion machinery.

claim: DRP-1 is required for mitochondrial fission.
source: In opposition to the activities of FZO-1 and EAT-3, DRP-1 is required for mitochondrial fission (Smirnova et al., 2001; Lima et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RNAi of fzo-1 reduced mitochondrial fusion in wild-type male sperm.
source: RNAi of fzo-1 or eat-3 reduced mitochondrial fusion in wild-type male sperm (Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) and suppressed the enhanced fusion observed in alh-6 mutant spermatid mitochondria (Figure 5K); indicating mitochondrial fusion of both membranes is active in spermatids with impaired proline catabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: RNAi of eat-3 reduced mitochondrial fusion in wild-type male sperm.
source: RNAi of fzo-1 or eat-3 reduced mitochondrial fusion in wild-type male sperm (Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) and suppressed the enhanced fusion observed in alh-6 mutant spermatid mitochondria (Figure 5K); indicating mitochondrial fusion of both membranes is active in spermatids with impaired proline catabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: RNAi of fzo-1 or eat-3 suppressed the enhanced fusion observed in alh-6 mutant spermatid mitochondria.
source: RNAi of fzo-1 or eat-3 reduced mitochondrial fusion in wild-type male sperm (Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) and suppressed the enhanced fusion observed in alh-6 mutant spermatid mitochondria (Figure 5K); indicating mitochondrial fusion of both membranes is active in spermatids with impaired proline catabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion of both membranes is active in spermatids with impaired proline catabolism.
source: RNAi of fzo-1 or eat-3 reduced mitochondrial fusion in wild-type male sperm (Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) and suppressed the enhanced fusion observed in alh-6 mutant spermatid mitochondria (Figure 5K); indicating mitochondrial fusion of both membranes is active in spermatids with impaired proline catabolism.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi experiments showing that both fzo-1 and eat-3 can suppress fusion in alh-6 mutants.

claim: Spermatids from drp-1 mutant animals have a greater level of mitochondrial fusion as compared to wild type and alh-6 mutant spermatids.
source: We next examined spermatids from drp-1 mutant animals and observed a greater level of mitochondrial fusion as compared to wild type and alh-6 mutant spermatids (Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: alh-6; drp-1 double mutants show a synergistic level of mitochondrial fusion in spermatids.
source: We also observed a synergistic level of mitochondrial fusion in spermatids derived from alh-6; drp-1 double mutants. This finding is consistent with previous studies in yeast which reveal that defects in fusion can be compensated for by changes in the rates of fission and vice versa (Shaw and Nunnari, 2002; van der Bliek et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of drp-1 reduces sperm activation.
source: In support of our model where mitochondrial dynamics act as a major driver of the sperm-specific defects in alh-6 mutants, we discovered that loss of drp-1, which results in increased mitochondrial fusion (like that observed in alh-6 mutants), also reduces sperm activation (Figure 5M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Reducing fzo-1 does not alter activation in wild type sperm.
source: Moreover, reducing fzo-1 or eat-3 does not alter activation in wild type sperm, while fzo-1 but not eat-3 RNAi restores activation in alh-6 sperm (Figure 5N–O and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), suggesting increased fusion mediated predominantly by fzo-1 in alh-6 sperm mitochondria is impairing proper function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: fzo-1 RNAi restores activation in alh-6 sperm.
source: Moreover, reducing fzo-1 or eat-3 does not alter activation in wild type sperm, while fzo-1 but not eat-3 RNAi restores activation in alh-6 sperm (Figure 5N–O and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), suggesting increased fusion mediated predominantly by fzo-1 in alh-6 sperm mitochondria is impairing proper function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: eat-3 RNAi does not restore activation in alh-6 sperm.
source: Moreover, reducing fzo-1 or eat-3 does not alter activation in wild type sperm, while fzo-1 but not eat-3 RNAi restores activation in alh-6 sperm (Figure 5N–O and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), suggesting increased fusion mediated predominantly by fzo-1 in alh-6 sperm mitochondria is impairing proper function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5O.

claim: Increased fusion mediated predominantly by fzo-1 in alh-6 sperm mitochondria is impairing proper function.
source: Moreover, reducing fzo-1 or eat-3 does not alter activation in wild type sperm, while fzo-1 but not eat-3 RNAi restores activation in alh-6 sperm (Figure 5N–O and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), suggesting increased fusion mediated predominantly by fzo-1 in alh-6 sperm mitochondria is impairing proper function.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of fzo-1 vs eat-3 RNAi on alh-6 sperm activation.

claim: alh-6 mutant animals have an increased expression of fzo-1 transcripts.
source: We noted that alh-6 mutant animals have an increased expression of fzo-1 transcripts that is suggestive of a retrograde signaling response from the mitochondria (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial proline catabolism induces mitochondrial stress, activating mitochondrial fusion, in order to dilute damage to preserve functional mitochondria at the cost of sperm function.
source: Taken together, these data support a model where loss of mitochondrial proline catabolism induces mitochondrial stress, activating mitochondrial fusion, in order to dilute damage to preserve functional mitochondria at the cost of sperm function.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the experimental data showing increased fusion in alh-6 mutants and rescue by reducing fusion.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion and fission have a functional role in spermatid development and sperm function.
source: These data also reveal a functional role for mitochondrial fusion and fission in spermatid development and sperm function.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that manipulating fusion/fission machinery affects sperm activation.

claim: Germline specific RNAi of alh-6 in wild-type males was not sufficient to alter sperm size.
source: Germline specific RNAi of alh-6 in wild-type males was not sufficient to alter sperm size (Figure 6A), but did result in diminished sperm activation (Figure 6B,) and increased mitochondrial fusion in sperm (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Germline specific RNAi of alh-6 in wild-type males resulted in diminished sperm activation.
source: Germline specific RNAi of alh-6 in wild-type males was not sufficient to alter sperm size (Figure 6A), but did result in diminished sperm activation (Figure 6B,) and increased mitochondrial fusion in sperm (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Germline specific RNAi of alh-6 in wild-type males resulted in increased mitochondrial fusion in sperm.
source: Germline specific RNAi of alh-6 in wild-type males was not sufficient to alter sperm size (Figure 6A), but did result in diminished sperm activation (Figure 6B,) and increased mitochondrial fusion in sperm (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: RNAi of alh-6 only in the soma resulted in a minor reduction of spermatid size.
source: Similarly, RNAi of alh-6 only in the soma resulted in a minor reduction of spermatid size (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), but did not phenocopy the impairment of sperm activation as observed in alh-6 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RNAi of alh-6 only in the soma did not phenocopy the impairment of sperm activation as observed in alh-6 mutants.
source: Similarly, RNAi of alh-6 only in the soma resulted in a minor reduction of spermatid size (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), but did not phenocopy the impairment of sperm activation as observed in alh-6 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Somatic expression of alh-6 can influence spermatid size.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that somatic expression of alh-6 can influence spermatid size while the influence of alh-6 on spermatid activation is cell autonomous.
evidence: This is inferred from the soma-specific RNAi experiments showing a minor effect on sperm size.

claim: The influence of alh-6 on spermatid activation is cell autonomous.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that somatic expression of alh-6 can influence spermatid size while the influence of alh-6 on spermatid activation is cell autonomous.
evidence: This is inferred from the germline-specific RNAi experiments showing impaired activation.

claim: Germline specific rescue of WT alh-6 in alh-6 mutant male animals restored sperm size in one of the two transgenic lines.
source: Next, we restored wild-type alh-6 expression, only in the germline, in alh-6 mutant animals, which restored sperm size in one of the two transgenic lines (Figure 6D), activation (Figure 6E) and mitochondrial dynamics (Figure 6F), as compared to non-transgenic siblings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Germline specific rescue of WT alh-6 in alh-6 mutant male animals restored activation.
source: Next, we restored wild-type alh-6 expression, only in the germline, in alh-6 mutant animals, which restored sperm size in one of the two transgenic lines (Figure 6D), activation (Figure 6E) and mitochondrial dynamics (Figure 6F), as compared to non-transgenic siblings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Germline specific rescue of WT alh-6 in alh-6 mutant male animals restored mitochondrial dynamics.
source: Next, we restored wild-type alh-6 expression, only in the germline, in alh-6 mutant animals, which restored sperm size in one of the two transgenic lines (Figure 6D), activation (Figure 6E) and mitochondrial dynamics (Figure 6F), as compared to non-transgenic siblings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The effects of loss of alh-6 on sperm function (activation and mitochondria) are cell autonomous.
source: We conclude that the effects of loss of alh-6 on sperm function (activation and mitochondria) are cell autonomous because germline specific RNAi could phenocopy the sperm defects observed in whole animal loss of alh-6, while RNAi of alh-6 only in the somatic tissues could not.
evidence: This is inferred from the germline-specific RNAi and rescue experiments.

claim: The effect of alh-6 on sperm size is non-cell autonomous and requires somatic input.
source: In contrast, the effect of alh-6 on sperm size is non-cell autonomous and requires somatic input (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that germline-specific RNAi does not affect sperm size while soma-specific RNAi does.

claim: Germline knockdown of R10H10.6 phenocopies germline knockdown of alh-6 on sperm size, sperm activation, and mitochondrial fusion in sperm.
source: Similarly, we reduced R10H10.6 or flad-1 only in the germline, which phenocopies germline knockdown of alh-6 on sperm size (Figure 6G,J), sperm activation (Figure 6H,K), and mitochondrial fusion in sperm (Figure 6I,L), as observed in whole animal RNAi of flad-1 or R10H10.6 (Figure 4J–K and Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G-I.

claim: Germline knockdown of flad-1 phenocopies germline knockdown of alh-6 on sperm size, sperm activation, and mitochondrial fusion in sperm.
source: Similarly, we reduced R10H10.6 or flad-1 only in the germline, which phenocopies germline knockdown of alh-6 on sperm size (Figure 6G,J), sperm activation (Figure 6H,K), and mitochondrial fusion in sperm (Figure 6I,L), as observed in whole animal RNAi of flad-1 or R10H10.6 (Figure 4J–K and Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6J-L.

claim: FAD functions in cell autonomously regulating sperm function (activation and mitochondrial dynamics).
source: These results suggest that FAD functions similarly to alh-6 in cell autonomously regulating sperm function (activation and mitochondrial dynamics), while affecting sperm size in a cell non-autonomous manner (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: This is inferred from the germline-specific RNAi experiments of FAD biosynthesis genes.

claim: FAD affects sperm size in a cell non-autonomous manner.
source: These results suggest that FAD functions similarly to alh-6 in cell autonomously regulating sperm function (activation and mitochondrial dynamics), while affecting sperm size in a cell non-autonomous manner (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that germline-specific RNAi of FAD biosynthesis genes does not affect sperm size.

claim: Proline catabolism and FAD homeostasis in germ cells are important to maintain proper sperm function.
source: Taken together these data identify the importance of proline catabolism and FAD homeostasis in germ cells to maintain proper sperm function.
evidence: This is inferred from the germline-specific experiments showing that both pathways are required in germ cells for proper sperm function.

claim: Exposure to pollution, toxins, xenobiotics, and other ROS-inducing compounds can prematurely drive the loss of sperm function across species.
source: Decades of work have shown that exposure to pollution, toxins, xenobiotics, and other ROS-inducing compounds can prematurely drive the loss of sperm function across species (Agarwal et al., 2014; Wagner et al., 2018; Cocuzza et al., 2007), but the impact that normal cellular metabolism plays on sperm function and the identification of specific molecules that can mediate sperm quality are not well-defined.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The impact that normal cellular metabolism plays on sperm function and the identification of specific molecules that can mediate sperm quality are not well-defined.
source: Decades of work have shown that exposure to pollution, toxins, xenobiotics, and other ROS-inducing compounds can prematurely drive the loss of sperm function across species (Agarwal et al., 2014; Wagner et al., 2018; Cocuzza et al., 2007), but the impact that normal cellular metabolism plays on sperm function and the identification of specific molecules that can mediate sperm quality are not well-defined.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in current knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: Mutation in proline dehydrogenase (PRODH) in humans results in hyperprolinemia type I (HPI).
source: Mutation in proline dehydrogenase (PRODH) in humans results in hyperprolinemia type I (HPI), while mutation in delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate dehydrogenase (ALDH4A1/P5CDH) results in hyperprolinemia type II (HPII).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about genetic disorders.

claim: Mutation in delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate dehydrogenase (ALDH4A1/P5CDH) in humans results in hyperprolinemia type II (HPII).
source: Mutation in proline dehydrogenase (PRODH) in humans results in hyperprolinemia type I (HPI), while mutation in delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate dehydrogenase (ALDH4A1/P5CDH) results in hyperprolinemia type II (HPII).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about genetic disorders.

claim: In C. elegans, proline catabolism impacts several functional qualities of male sperm.
source: This study reveals that in C. elegans, proline catabolism impacts several functional qualities of male sperm.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data in the study.

claim: Loss of proline catabolism results in smaller sperm with impaired activation, two qualities that directly impact competitive advantage.
source: Loss of proline catabolism results in smaller sperm with impaired activation, two qualities that directly impact competitive advantage.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing reduced sperm size and activation in alh-6 mutants.

claim: Proline biosynthesis, catabolism, and steady state concentrations must be tightly regulated.
source: As such, proline biosynthesis, catabolism, and steady state concentrations must be tightly regulated, and the importance of proline in cellular homeostasis may help explain the transcriptional responses measured in animals with dysfunctional alh-6.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing transcriptional changes in alh-6 mutants.

claim: Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) is a precursor to the FAD and FMN cofactors that are needed for metabolic reactions in order to maintain proper cellular function.
source: Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) is a precursor to the FAD and FMN cofactors that are needed for metabolic reactions in order to maintain proper cellular function, like proline catabolism and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Humans lack a riboflavin biosynthetic pathway and therefore require riboflavin from exogenous sources.
source: Despite its importance, humans, like C. elegans, lack a riboflavin biosynthetic pathway and therefore require riboflavin from exogenous sources (Powers, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Insufficient riboflavin intake can lead to impairment of flavin homeostasis, which is associated with cancer, cardiovascular diseases, anemia, neurological disorders, impaired fetal development, etc.
source: Insufficient intake can lead to impairment of flavin homeostasis, which is associated with cancer, cardiovascular diseases, anemia, neurological disorders, impaired fetal development, etc. (Powers, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Riboflavin and FAD play critical roles in reproduction, specifically in germ cell development.
source: Our study suggests that riboflavin and FAD play critical roles in reproduction, specifically in germ cell development, as loss of FAD biosynthesis or loss of alh-6 specifically in the germline recapitulates the sperm defects observed in whole animal knockdown or alh-6 mutation.
evidence: This is inferred from the germline-specific experiments showing that FAD is required in germ cells for proper sperm function.

claim: Sperm-specific defects can be corrected by dietary supplementation of vitamin B2.
source: Importantly, these sperm-specific defects can be corrected by dietary supplementation of vitamin B2, which in light of the exceptional conservation of mitochondrial homeostatic pathways, suggest the nutraceutical role vitamin B2 could play in sperm health across species.
evidence: This is supported by the riboflavin supplementation experiments showing rescue of sperm defects.

claim: The exceptional conservation of mitochondrial homeostatic pathways suggests the nutraceutical role vitamin B2 could play in sperm health across species.
source: Importantly, these sperm-specific defects can be corrected by dietary supplementation of vitamin B2, which in light of the exceptional conservation of mitochondrial homeostatic pathways, suggest the nutraceutical role vitamin B2 could play in sperm health across species.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the conservation of pathways and the experimental results in C. elegans.

claim: Spermatids lacking alh-6 have increased mitochondrial fusion.
source: Our study also demonstrates that spermatids lacking alh-6 have increased mitochondrial fusion; a perturbation at the mitochondrial organelle structure-level that contributes to the sperm-specific phenotypes observed.
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy data showing increased mitochondrial fusion in alh-6 mutant spermatids.

claim: Increased mitochondrial fusion contributes to the sperm-specific phenotypes observed in alh-6 mutants.
source: Our study also demonstrates that spermatids lacking alh-6 have increased mitochondrial fusion; a perturbation at the mitochondrial organelle structure-level that contributes to the sperm-specific phenotypes observed.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing that reducing fusion can rescue sperm activation defects.

claim: Mitochondrial fission and fusion machinery are present and active in spermatids.
source: In addition to prior work showing fzo-1/MFN1/MFN2 and drp-1/DRP-1 to be important for mitochondrial elimination post-fertilization (Wang et al., 2016), our work reveals that mitochondrial fission and fusion machinery are present and active in spermatids and that perturbation of these dynamics can affect sperm maturation and competitive fitness.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing that manipulating fusion/fission machinery affects sperm function.

claim: Perturbation of mitochondrial dynamics can affect sperm maturation and competitive fitness.
source: In addition to prior work showing fzo-1/MFN1/MFN2 and drp-1/DRP-1 to be important for mitochondrial elimination post-fertilization (Wang et al., 2016), our work reveals that mitochondrial fission and fusion machinery are present and active in spermatids and that perturbation of these dynamics can affect sperm maturation and competitive fitness.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing that altering fusion/fission affects sperm activation and competitive advantage.

claim: Proline metabolism is a major metabolic pathway that can impact sperm maturation and male reproductive success.
source: In conclusion, our work identifies proline metabolism as a major metabolic pathway that can impact sperm maturation and male reproductive success.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by all the experimental data in the study.

claim: Specific interventions can reverse the redox imbalance, cofactor depletion, and altered mitochondria dynamics that play a part in sperm dysfunction resulting from proline metabolism defects.
source: Moreover, these studies identify specific interventions to reverse the redox imbalance, cofactor depletion, and altered mitochondria dynamics, all of which play a part in sperm dysfunction resulting from proline metabolism defects.
evidence: This is supported by the riboflavin supplementation and genetic manipulation experiments showing rescue of sperm defects.
